main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of business
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the principles of business
learning_activity_name: Describe the basic aspects of business environment (stakeholders in business and agents supporting business start-ups)
sla_name: Business Environment: Stakeholders and Start-up Agents
sla_teaching_aids: Online/ offline sources|Bronchers from Tanzania National Business Council (TNBC)|Tanzania Chamber of Commerce|Industry|Agriculiture (TCCIA)
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The business environment is everything inside and outside a business that affects how it operates. Stakeholders and supporting agents strongly influence whether a new business survives.
sla_notes_details: Stakeholders are individuals or groups with an interest in the business: owners, employees, customers, suppliers, creditors, competitors, government, local community and financial institutions. Internal factors are owners, staff, resources and management style, while external factors follow the PESTEL headings (political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal). Agents that support business start-ups in Tanzania include the Tanzania National Business Council (TNBC), the Tanzania Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture (TCCIA), the Small Industries Development Organisation (SIDO), the Business Registrations and Licensing Agency (BRELA), the Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA), banks, microfinance institutions and business incubators. They give advice, training, registration, financing and markets.
sla_notes_illustrations: A young person planning a poultry business identifies customers (restaurants), suppliers (feed sellers), competitors (other farmers), TRA (tax), BRELA (registration) and SIDO (training), and lists how each will affect the business.
sla_notes_daily_life: Every shop, kiosk or market stall works within a business environment; a change in fuel price or new tax rule affects the price of goods sold.
sla_exercise: Who are business stakeholders? Give two examples.::People or groups with an interest in a business, such as customers and employees.||Name two agents that support business start-ups in Tanzania.::SIDO and BRELA (also TCCIA, TNBC, TRA).||What does PESTEL stand for?::Political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal factors.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of business
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the principles of business
learning_activity_name: Describe some advanced aspects of the business units (size classification, company and company’s management, franchise, joint ventures and cooperatives, formation and dissolution)
sla_assessment_criteria: Some advanced aspects of the business units clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Company Act|Videos/ trade shows|Online/ offline sources
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Business units are organisations that produce or sell goods and services, and they differ in size, ownership and structure. Medium businesses often choose forms such as companies, franchises, joint ventures and cooperatives.
sla_notes_details: Businesses are classified by size using employees, capital and turnover (micro, small, medium and large, per the SME policy). A company is a legal entity separate from its owners, with limited liability; private companies restrict share transfer while public companies can sell shares to the public, and management is by a board of directors and managers who report to shareholders. A franchise is an agreement in which a franchisor allows a franchisee to use its brand and system for a fee (for example a fast-food outlet). A joint venture is a partnership between two or more firms for a specific project, sharing capital, risk and profit. A cooperative is owned and controlled by members on the principle of one member one vote. Formation involves steps like drafting the memorandum and articles of association and registration with BRELA, and dissolution can be voluntary or by court order, bankruptcy or expiry of an agreed term.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group of farmers forms a cooperative society, registers it, contributes shares, elects a board and sells maize together, sharing profits by the amount of produce each member supplied.
sla_notes_daily_life: Well-known franchises and cooperative societies (such as SACCOS) in the local town show these business units at work.
sla_exercise: What is limited liability?::A shareholder's loss is limited to the amount invested in the company.||Define a franchise.::An agreement allowing a person to use another firm's brand and business system for a fee.||Which principle applies in cooperatives?::One member one vote.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of business
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the principles of business
learning_activity_name: Describe some advanced aspects of financing medium businesses (internal and external sources: retained earnings, sale and leaseback of non-current assets, share capital, venture capital, overdrafts, loans, debentures, crowd funding and government grants)
sla_name: Advanced Aspects of Financing Medium Businesses
sla_assessment_criteria: Some advanced aspects of financing medium businesses clearly described.
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Financing means obtaining money to start, operate and expand a business. Medium businesses use internal and external sources and must choose the cheapest suitable one.
sla_notes_details: Internal sources are retained earnings (profits kept in the business) and sale and leaseback of non-current assets, where an asset is sold and leased back to release cash. External sources include share capital (issuing shares), venture capital (funds from investors for growth in return for equity), overdrafts (short-term borrowing on a current account), loans (repaid with interest), debentures (long-term borrowing certificates paying fixed interest), crowd funding (small sums from many people via online platforms) and government grants (funds that need not be repaid). Factors in choosing include cost of finance, period, risk, control retained, repayment ability and security required.
sla_notes_illustrations: A bakery needs TSh 20 million for an oven: it uses TSh 5 million from retained earnings and takes a bank loan of TSh 15 million repayable in three years with 16 percent interest.
sla_notes_daily_life: Many local entrepreneurs finance their shops through savings, SACCOS loans, mobile-money-based lending or family contributions.
sla_exercise: What are retained earnings?::Profits kept in the business instead of being distributed.||Differentiate an overdraft from a loan.::An overdraft is short-term borrowing on a current account, while a loan is a fixed sum repaid over an agreed period.||Give one advantage of government grants.::They do not have to be repaid.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the business environment
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the policies and laws governing medium scale business
learning_activity_name: Explore the basic aspects of the policy and regulatory environment governing medium businesses in Tanzania (roles of government and non-governmental agencies, policies, laws and by-laws)
sla_name: Policy and Regulatory Environment of Medium Businesses
sla_assessment_criteria: Basic aspects of the policy and regulatory environment governing medium sized businesses in Tanzania are effectively explored.
sla_teaching_aids: Online/ offline sources|Rules|Regulations|Policies governing business in Tanzania
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Government policies, laws and by-laws control how businesses operate. Students explore who makes these rules and how they affect business owners.
sla_notes_details: The government (ministries such as Industry and Trade) and non-governmental agencies (such as TCCIA, TNBC and consumer groups) shape the business environment. Key policies include the SME Development Policy and the Industrial Policy, while laws include the Companies Act, the Business Licensing Act, the Income Tax Act, labour and environmental laws, and local government by-laws on market fees and hygiene. Roles of government include regulating, providing infrastructure, giving incentives, protecting consumers and collecting taxes. Non-governmental bodies lobby, train members and provide information.
sla_notes_illustrations: A trader opening a restaurant must follow health regulations from the municipal council, pay licence fees, follow employment law and keep records for tax authorities, showing policies, laws and by-laws at work.
sla_notes_daily_life: By-laws about waste disposal and market places affect small traders in every town every day.
sla_exercise: Give one role of government in business.::Regulating business activities or providing infrastructure.||What is a by-law?::A rule made by a local authority for its area.||Name one non-governmental agency that supports business in Tanzania.::TCCIA.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the business environment
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the policies and laws governing medium scale business
learning_activity_name: Describe procedures for registering medium businesses in Tanzania (types of licences, importance of registration and sanctions for non-compliance)
sla_assessment_criteria: Procedures for registering medium sized businesses in Tanzania is clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Procedures guide book for registration|Sample of application form for registration|Company Act|The Business Activities Registration Act|Business registration guide book|Online/ offline sources
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Registration gives a business legal recognition and access to formal services. Every business must follow the procedures required by law.
sla_notes_details: Steps are choosing and reserving a business name, preparing the required documents (memorandum and articles of association for companies, identification of directors), submitting them to BRELA (online), paying fees, obtaining a certificate, then obtaining a Tax Identification Number (TIN) from TRA and licences from local authorities and regulators. Types of licences are trade, industrial, professional and specialised licences (for example food or transport). Importance includes legal protection, access to loans and tenders, credibility and enforcement of contracts. Sanctions for non-compliance include fines, closure, seizure of goods and prosecution.
sla_notes_illustrations: A tailor starting a garment factory reserves a name, registers a company with BRELA, obtains a TIN from TRA and a business licence from the local authority before starting production.
sla_notes_daily_life: A registered business can open a bank account and sell to government institutions, which informal businesses often cannot.
sla_exercise: Which agency registers companies in Tanzania?::BRELA.||Name two types of licences.::Trade licence and industrial licence.||State one sanction for operating without registration.::A fine or closure of the business.

main_competence_name: Conduct a project in Business Studies
specific_competence_name: Prepare a medium scale business plan
learning_activity_name: Identify an appropriate business opportunity and develop its business plan
sla_name: Identifying a Business Opportunity and Developing a Business Plan
sla_assessment_criteria: Business opportunity identified and its business plan developed.
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A business plan is a written document that shows what the business will do, how it will do it and how it will earn money. It begins with identifying a good opportunity.
sla_notes_details: Opportunities are found by studying community needs, market gaps, resources available and trends using brainstorming, SWOT analysis and market surveys. A business plan has a cover page, executive summary, business description, market analysis, marketing plan, operations plan, management and organisation, financial plan (start-up costs, cash flow forecast, profit projections and break-even) and risk analysis. Students prepare it in groups and present it for feedback.
sla_notes_illustrations: Students find that their school area lacks a stationery and photocopy shop, calculate start-up cost of TSh 3 million, forecast monthly income and prepare the plan.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same plan is submitted to banks or SACCOS when seeking a loan to start a real business.
sla_exercise: Name two methods of identifying a business opportunity.::Market survey and SWOT analysis.||What does the financial plan contain?::Start-up costs, cash flow forecasts and profit projections.||Why is a business plan important?::It guides the owner and convinces lenders and investors.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of business
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the principles of business
learning_activity_name: Describe some basic aspects of operations management (methods of production, value addition and stock administration)
sla_name: Operations Management: Production, Value Addition and Stock
sla_assessment_criteria: Concept of operations management clearly explained.
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Operations management is the planning and controlling of the processes that turn inputs into goods and services. It aims for quality, low cost and timely delivery.
sla_notes_details: Methods of production are job (one item made to order), batch (groups of items), and flow or mass production (continuous production). Value addition means increasing the worth of a product through processing, packaging, branding and grading (for example turning cashew nuts into roasted packaged snacks). Stock administration involves controlling raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods by determining reorder level, economic order quantity, maximum and minimum levels, and methods such as FIFO, LIFO and just-in-time. Good stock control avoids shortages, wastage and tied-up capital.
sla_notes_illustrations: A juice producer uses batch production, adds value by pasteurising and bottling with a label, and orders new bottles when stock falls to the reorder level of 500 units.
sla_notes_daily_life: A shopkeeper who sells oldest flour first (FIFO) and reorders sugar before it runs out is applying stock administration.
sla_exercise: Name three methods of production.::Job, batch and flow production.||What is value addition?::Increasing the worth of a product through processing, packaging or branding.||What does FIFO mean?::First in, first out, meaning the oldest stock is used or sold first.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of business
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the principles of business
learning_activity_name: Explain some aspects of insurance for medium businesses (choice of appropriate insurance plan and procedures for filing insurance claims)
sla_assessment_criteria: Some aspects of insurance for medium businesses properly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Online/offline sources|Insurance documents (guides / fliers / claim application form|Cover note)|Bank|Financial Institutions Act
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Insurance transfers the financial risk of loss from a business to an insurance company in return for a premium. Choosing the right plan protects the business.
sla_notes_details: Common types are fire, burglary, goods in transit, fidelity guarantee, motor, public liability, marine and employees' compensation insurance. Principles include utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, contribution, subrogation and proximate cause. Choosing a plan involves identifying risks, comparing premiums, cover, exclusions and reputation of insurers, and deciding on a sum insured. To file a claim the insured reports the loss promptly, completes a claim form, provides supporting evidence (police report, receipts), allows an assessor to inspect and then receives compensation.
sla_notes_illustrations: A warehouse owner insures stock worth TSh 40 million against fire; after a fire he reports within 48 hours, submits the claim form, receipts and fire report and is paid after assessment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Insuring a delivery motorcycle or a shop stock is a practical way small traders protect themselves from unexpected losses.
sla_exercise: What is a premium?::The amount paid to an insurer for cover.||State the principle of indemnity.::The insured must be restored to the same financial position as before the loss, but not better.||Name two documents used when claiming for burglary.::Claim form and police report.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of business
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the principles of business
learning_activity_name: Describe some advanced aspects of marketing (marketing mix - 4Cs and 7Ps, market changes, market segmentation, marketing boards, market research, e-marketing)
sla_assessment_criteria: Some advanced aspects of marketing clearly described.
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Marketing identifies and satisfies customer needs profitably. Advanced marketing covers the marketing mix, segmentation, research and modern e-marketing.
sla_notes_details: The traditional marketing mix has the 4Cs (customer needs, cost to the customer, convenience and communication) that correspond to the 4Ps of product, price, place and promotion; services add people, process and physical evidence, giving 7Ps. Market changes come from tastes, income, technology and competition. Market segmentation divides a market by geography, demography, behaviour or psychographics so that each group can be targeted. Marketing boards (for example for cotton or cashew) organise the buying, grading and selling of commodities. Market research collects primary and secondary data by questionnaires, interviews and observation. E-marketing uses websites, social media, mobile money and email.
sla_notes_illustrations: A mobile phone accessories seller segments by age, targets students with low-priced cases advertised on WhatsApp and Instagram and uses a customer questionnaire to decide the next products.
sla_notes_daily_life: Every advertisement on the radio or social media that a consumer sees applies the principles of the marketing mix.
sla_exercise: List the 4Ps.::Product, price, place and promotion.||What is market segmentation?::Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs.||Give one advantage of e-marketing.::It reaches many customers at low cost.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of business
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the principles of business
learning_activity_name: Explore the basic aspects of law of contract (nature of contractual obligations, elements of a contract, formation of a contract, types of misrepresentation, forms and consequences of breach of contract and remedies for breach)
sla_assessment_criteria: Basic aspects of law of contract effectively explored.
sla_teaching_aids: The Law of Contract Act|Samples of contracts|Online/ offline sources
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A contract is an agreement enforceable by law. It governs many business dealings from sales to employment.
sla_notes_details: Under the Law of Contract Act a valid contract needs offer, acceptance, intention to create legal relations, consideration, capacity of parties, free consent and legality of purpose. Formation happens when an offer is accepted unconditionally and communicated. Types of misrepresentation are innocent, negligent and fraudulent, and they may make the contract voidable. Contracts may be written, oral, express, implied, simple or contracts under seal. Breach occurs when a party fails to perform; consequences include damages, and remedies are damages, specific performance, injunction, rescission and quantum meruit.
sla_notes_illustrations: A trader agrees in writing to supply 100 bags of rice at TSh 90,000 each; if the trader does not deliver, the buyer may sue for damages equal to the extra cost of buying elsewhere.
sla_notes_daily_life: Buying goods, renting a house, hiring a worker and taking a loan all create contracts.
sla_exercise: Name two elements of a valid contract.::Offer and acceptance (also consideration, capacity).||What is a remedy for breach of contract? Give one.::Damages or specific performance.||Name the three types of misrepresentation.::Innocent, negligent and fraudulent.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the business environment
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the policies and laws governing medium scale businesses
learning_activity_name: Describe taxes and levies associated with medium businesses in Tanzania
sla_name: Taxes and Levies for Medium Businesses
sla_assessment_criteria: Taxes and levies associated with medium businesses in Tanzania clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Tax clearance certificate|TRA guide flier|Income Tax Act|Value-Added Act|Online/ offline sources
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Taxes are compulsory payments to government while levies are charges for specific purposes. Businesses must calculate, record and pay them correctly.
sla_notes_details: Taxes include corporate income tax, value added tax (VAT, 18 percent), pay as you earn (PAYE), withholding tax, customs duty, excise duty and stamp duty. Levies include skills and development levy, local government service levy and fire levy. Direct taxes are paid by the person who bears them and indirect taxes are passed on to consumers. Businesses register with TRA, get a TIN, issue electronic fiscal device receipts, keep records and file returns on time. Taxes finance public services and non-compliance brings penalties.
sla_notes_illustrations: A supplier sells goods for TSh 1,000,000 plus 18 percent VAT, so the customer pays TSh 1,180,000 and the supplier remits TSh 180,000 to TRA.
sla_notes_daily_life: A shopper who receives an EFD receipt is paying tax that funds roads, schools and hospitals.
sla_exercise: Give one example of a direct tax.::Income tax or PAYE.||What is the standard rate of VAT in Tanzania?::18 percent.||Which authority collects taxes in Tanzania?::The Tanzania Revenue Authority.

main_competence_name: Conduct a project in Business Studies
specific_competence_name: Prepare a medium scale business plan
learning_activity_name: Complete and submit the business plan developed in Form Five
sla_name: Completing and Submitting the Business Plan
sla_references: TET(2023), BUSINESS STUDIES SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Form Six students finish the business plan started in Form Five and submit it for assessment. Presentations enable feedback.
sla_notes_details: Students review the market analysis, operations, marketing plan and financial statements, correct errors, add an executive summary and appendices and check that costs, prices and forecasts are realistic. They present and defend the plan to the class in a business plan presentation week, respond to questions and submit the final copy. Assessment considers feasibility, clarity, completeness and originality.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group that planned a small bakery updates its cash-flow forecast, shows break-even at 450 loaves per month and submits the final plan with a summary.
sla_notes_daily_life: A well-written plan can be used to apply for a loan, a grant or a business competition.
sla_exercise: What is added to the final business plan?::An executive summary and appendices.||Why do students present the plan?::To defend it and receive feedback.||Name one criterion for assessment of the plan.::Feasibility (or clarity, completeness).
